title: Buffer Overflow
description: Buffer Overflow is the 1998 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of industrial metal crossed with techno about keeping systems and people safe. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword plays lead guitar, Wyrd brings sequencers and acid synths, and Bytes plays live drums over programmed breakbeats and sings backup. The security triad, threat models, passwords and two-factor authentication, least privilege, buffer overflows, input validation, encryption, public keys, digital signatures, man-in-the-middle attacks and social engineering. Written after a fan walked backstage by saying “I’m with the duck.” Play loud. Trust no input.
tagline: The 1998 industrial-techno album from Procedural Byts: a computer security course in twelve songs, and why backstage passes now need two factors.
lineup: The four-piece, online. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays lead guitar. Wyrd plays synthesizers and sequencers. Bytes plays live drums over programmed breakbeats and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the band’s security officer, not by choice. Nyble sings lead on every song, plays bass, and holds the only private key.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits, and the owner of the longest password in the band. Qword’s solos on this album probe for weaknesses, scramble melodies, and run one bar past the end on purpose.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, now on sequencers, an acid bass synth and a drum machine. Wyrd once encrypted the setlist so well that nobody, Wyrd included, could read it for a week.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, playing live drums over breakbeats and singing backup. His password was “drums.” It isn’t anymore.

members.name: Null
members.bio: The most effective backstage pass in rock, until 1998. Now a security question. The answer is still nothing.

story.heading: I’m With the Duck
paragraphs: By 1998, the band was online: a fan site, a mailing list, and one shared email account whose password everyone knew. Wyrd had discovered techno and arrived at rehearsal with a sequencer, an acid bass synth and a drum machine. Bytes played live drums on top of the machine, louder than it, out of principle.

They decided it was time to take security seriously, and started by threat-modeling the tour. What are we protecting? The master tapes, the setlist, the duck. Who wants it? Bootleggers, a rival band, the label. How would they get it? The answer to almost every question was “the duck.”
Bytes’s password was “drums.” Then “drums1.” Then “Drums1!” Nyble sat him down and explained hashing, salting and passphrases. He now has a password nobody knows, including, some days, Bytes.

The master tapes went to the pressing plant in a locked case, with the key sent separately by a second courier. The case arrived first and sat at the plant for a week. For the next shipment, they used a lock anyone could close but only Nyble could open.

On the first night of the tour, a fan walked straight past security by smiling and saying, “I’m with the duck.” It worked. The band considers it their first social-engineering attack. Backstage passes now need two factors: the laminate, and the answer to a question. The question is “what does the duck say?” The answer is nothing.

cover_sub: The 1998 album. Every lock was perfect, until someone asked nicely.

songs.title: Triad

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Three things to guard and three things to keep,
Secrets stay secret while the others sleep.
The data stays true, no one changes a line,
And it’s there when you need it every time!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Confidentiality! (Keep it hidden!)
Integrity! (Keep it true!)
Availability! (Keep it running!)
The triad, the triad, protecting you!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Lock it up too tight and no one can get in,
Leave it wide open and the attackers win.
Every choice is a trade between the three,
Balance it right, and the system’s safe and free!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Read it? (Confidentiality!)
Change it? (Integrity!)
Reach it? (Availability!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd’s acid synth line has three sections: one played so quietly only the band can hear it, one that repeats exactly without a single changed note, and one that never stops, even when the rest of the band does. Secret, true and available.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Confidentiality! (Keep it hidden!)
Integrity! (Keep it true!)
Availability! (Keep it running!)
The triad, the triad, protecting you!

songs.note: Opens with the sound of the band’s first modem connecting to the internet, slowed down to half speed.
songs.lesson: Security goals are often summarized as the CIA triad. Confidentiality: only authorized people can read the data. Integrity: the data can’t be changed without authorization. Availability: the system works when people need it. Real designs balance these three against each other and against how easy the system is to use.

songs.title: Threat Model

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: What are you protecting, and who would want to take it?
How would they get in, and what would they do to break it?
Think like the attacker before the attacker thinks of you,
Find the weakest door before they walk on through!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Threat model! (Know your foe!)
Threat model! (Know where they’ll go!)
Assets, threats and the paths they’ll take,
Threat model, threat model, for everybody’s sake!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A single wall will fall, so build them one by one,
Layer after layer till the attacker’s done.
Defense in depth, the lock, the guard, the alarm,
If one of them fails, the others keep you from harm!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Who? (The attacker!) What? (The asset!)
How? (The attack surface!) Why? (Because they can!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword probes the song like an attacker, trying a different opening every two bars until one works. Then the rest of the band answers with layer after layer of riffs, so the opening Qword found leads only to another wall.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Threat model! (Know your foe!)
Threat model! (Know where they’ll go!)
Assets, threats and the paths they’ll take,
Threat model, threat model, for everybody’s sake!

songs.note: The band threat-modeled the 1998 tour. The answer to almost every question was “the duck.”
songs.lesson: Threat modeling asks four questions: what are you protecting (your assets), who might attack it, how they could get in (the attack surface), and which defenses fit. Defense in depth layers several independent protections, so a single failure doesn’t expose everything.

songs.title: Password

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Your password is your dog’s name and the year that you were born,
Anyone could guess it long before the night is worn.
A dictionary attack will try a million words an hour,
Short and simple passwords never had the power!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Password! (Make it long!)
Password! (Make it strong!)
Never store it plain, hash it with a salt,
Password, password, or the break-in is your fault!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The server never keeps the password, just a one-way hash,
Add a random salt so matching passwords never match.
Use a different one for every place you go,
Reuse it once, and one leak lets them all know!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Drums! (Too short!) Drums one! (Too weak!)
A long and random passphrase is the one you seek!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays a short, simple pattern, and Wyrd’s drum machine copies it perfectly within one bar: guessed. Then Bytes plays a long, unpredictable pattern, and the machine can’t keep up.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Password! (Make it long!)
Password! (Make it strong!)
Never store it plain, hash it with a salt,
Password, password, or the break-in is your fault!

songs.note: Bytes’s password was “drums.” Then “drums1.” Then “Drums1!” This song is the intervention.
songs.lesson: Passwords should be long, unpredictable (passphrases help) and different for every site, because reusing one lets a single breach unlock everything. Servers should never store the passwords themselves, only salted hashes made with slow password-hashing functions, so a stolen database can’t easily be reversed. Attackers always try dictionary words and previously leaked passwords first.

songs.title: Two Factor

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A password can be stolen and a password can be guessed,
So ask for something more before you let them through with the rest.
Something that you know and something that you hold,
Two keys for every door, or you stay out in the cold!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Two factor! (What you know!)
Two factor! (What you have!)
Steal just one and you’re still not in,
Two factor, two factor, it takes two to get in!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Something you know, the password in your head,
Something that you have, a token or a card instead,
Something that you are, your fingerprint or face,
Pick two of different kinds and you’ve secured the place!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: What’s the password? (Drums!)
What does the duck say? (Nothing!)

parts.label: Locked solo: Qword and Nyble
parts.desc: Qword’s solo stops every four bars and won’t continue until Nyble’s bass answers with the right phrase. Once, Wyrd tries to answer instead, with the right notes in the wrong voice, and the solo stays locked.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Two factor! (What you know!)
Two factor! (What you have!)
Steal just one and you’re still not in,
Two factor, two factor, it takes two to get in!

songs.note: After the night in the story, backstage passes needed two factors: the pass, and the answer to a question. The question is “what does the duck say?”
songs.lesson: Multi-factor authentication asks for proof from two different categories: something you know (a password), something you have (a card, a token, a phone) and something you are (a fingerprint or face). Stealing one factor is no longer enough, which stops most password theft.

songs.title: Least Privilege

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The roadie gets the van keys but he doesn’t get the safe,
The intern gets the mailing list and nothing else to chafe.
Give everyone the smallest set of keys to do their part,
So when a key gets stolen, it can’t break the heart!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Least privilege! (Only what you need!)
Least privilege! (No more keys!)
Every user, every program, the smallest set of rights,
Least privilege, and the damage stays small at night!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Authentication says who you are, authorization what you may,
An access list on every file says read or write or stay away.
Don’t run it as the superuser just because it’s quick to do,
When it breaks, it breaks with every key you gave it too!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Read! (Yes.) Write! (No.)
Admin! (Never.)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo is only allowed three notes. Halfway through she needs a fourth, asks for it, gets it for exactly one bar, and gives it back.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Least privilege! (Only what you need!)
Least privilege! (No more keys!)
Every user, every program, the smallest set of rights,
Least privilege, and the damage stays small at night!

songs.note: Recorded with the studio’s door codes changed for every session. Only the engineer had all of them.
songs.lesson: Authentication establishes who you are; authorization decides what you’re allowed to do, often with access control lists or roles. The principle of least privilege gives every user and program only the permissions it actually needs, so if one is compromised the damage stays small. Don’t run things as an administrator just because it’s easier.

songs.title: Buffer Overflow

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Sixteen bytes of buffer and you hand me thirty-two,
I copy every one of them, I never check, it’s true.
The extra spills past the edge onto the memory next door,
Overwriting what was there, and it’s not what it was before!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Buffer overflow! (Too much!)
Buffer overflow! (Over the edge!)
Write past the end and you write over the rest,
Buffer overflow, check the length, it’s the only test!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Overwrite the return address and the program jumps away,
Running someone else’s code, and that’s a very bad day.
Check the bounds on every copy, never trust the size,
Use a language that won’t let it happen, and you’ll be wise!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Bounds check! (Bounds check!) Know where the buffer ends!
Memory safe! (Memory safe!) The language defends!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s solo is given eight bars. Qword plays nine. The ninth bar spills into the start of the next verse and overwrites Nyble’s first line, and the band has to stop and restart.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Buffer overflow! (Too much!)
Buffer overflow! (Over the edge!)
Write past the end and you write over the rest,
Buffer overflow, check the length, it’s the only test!
Buffer overflow!

songs.note: The title track. The last chorus is deliberately one line too long.
songs.lesson: A buffer overflow writes more data into a fixed-size buffer than it can hold, overwriting the memory next to it. That can crash the program, or let an attacker take control, for example by overwriting the address a function returns to. Prevent it by checking lengths, using safe library functions, and choosing memory-safe languages that check bounds automatically.

songs.title: Sanitize

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: You typed your name into the box and the box believed you,
But your name had a quote in it and a command or two.
The program pasted it straight into a query on the fly,
And the database obeyed it and it never asked why!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Sanitize! (Never trust the input!)
Sanitize! (Check it at the door!)
Every field and every form and every byte from the outside,
Sanitize, sanitize, and there’s nowhere for the code to hide!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Don’t glue the input into commands like it’s a piece of code,
Use parameters and keep the data on its own road.
Validate what you expect, reject what you do not,
Escape it on the way back out or the page will run their plot!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Name! (A name!) Number! (A number!)
Anything else! (Rejected!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Bytes throws a stream of random noise at Wyrd’s synth. Wyrd passes through only the notes that belong in the key and drops everything else before it can reach the rest of the band.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Sanitize! (Never trust the input!)
Sanitize! (Check it at the door!)
Every field and every form and every byte from the outside,
Sanitize, sanitize, and there’s nowhere for the code to hide!

songs.note: A callback to Third Normal Form. The database is fine. The input is the problem.
songs.lesson: Never trust input that comes from users or other systems. Injection attacks, like SQL injection, happen when input gets pasted into a command and treated as code. Defend by checking input against what you expect, using parameterized queries that keep data separate from code, and escaping output, for example when putting text on a web page.

songs.title: Encryption

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Scramble every message with a key that we both share,
Anyone who reads it hears just noise up in the air.
Use the same key to unlock it on the other side,
Symmetric encryption, and the meaning’s safe inside!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Encryption! (Lock it up!)
Encryption! (Scramble it all!)
Plaintext in and ciphertext out, a wall that won’t fall,
Encryption, encryption, and the key is all!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The algorithm can be public, everyone can know the plan,
The only secret is the key, so keep it if you can.
But how do I get the key to you without someone seeing it too?
That’s the problem no lock can solve, until something new!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Plaintext! (Readable!) Ciphertext! (Noise!)
The key! (The only secret!) Long! (There’s no other choice!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays a melody everyone knows, then plays it again scrambled by a pattern only Nyble knows. To everyone else it sounds like noise. Nyble applies the same pattern in reverse on her bass, and the original melody comes back out.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Encryption! (Lock it up!)
Encryption! (Scramble it all!)
Plaintext in and ciphertext out, a wall that won’t fall,
Encryption, encryption, and the key is all!

songs.note: The master tapes went to the pressing plant in a locked case, with the key sent by a different courier. The case arrived first and sat there for a week.
songs.lesson: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key both to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext and to turn it back. The algorithm can be public; only the key has to be secret (Kerckhoffs’s principle), and it must be long enough that trying every key is hopeless. The hard part is getting the key to the other person safely.

songs.title: Public Key

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I give the world a padlock and I keep the only key,
Anyone can lock a box and send it straight to me.
The public key is everywhere, I print it on the sleeve,
The private one stays home with me and never will it leave!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Public key! (Lock it with mine!)
Private key! (Only I can read the line!)
Two keys born together, one for all and one for one,
Public key, private key, and the sharing problem’s done!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Multiply two giant primes, a number huge and wide,
Easy to make but nearly impossible to divide.
Use it to send a session key, then switch to something fast,
The public key solves the handshake, and the secret’s safe at last!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Encrypt with the public! (Anyone can!)
Decrypt with the private! (Only one hand!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays a lead line that anyone in the band can join in and play along with. But only Nyble knows the closing phrase that resolves it, and when she plays it, the whole line suddenly makes sense.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Public key! (Lock it with mine!)
Private key! (Only I can read the line!)
Two keys born together, one for all and one for one,
Public key, private key, and the sharing problem’s done!

songs.note: The solution to the master-tape problem: a lock anyone can close, but only Nyble can open.
songs.lesson: Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography uses a pair of keys: anything locked with the public key can only be unlocked with the matching private key. Anyone can send you a secret without sharing one first. RSA’s security rests on how hard it is to factor the product of two huge primes. In practice, public keys are used to agree on a fast symmetric key for the rest of the conversation.

songs.title: Signed

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Run the message through a hash and a fingerprint comes out,
Change a single letter and the fingerprint will shout.
One way only, you can’t turn it back around,
The same input, the same hash, every time it’s found!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Signed! (It came from me!)
Signed! (It’s what I wrote!)
Sign it with my private key and anyone can check the note,
Signed, signed, sealed and true,
Nobody can forge my name, not even you!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Sign the hash with my private key, and that’s the signature,
Anyone with my public key can check that it is pure.
If the message changed along the way, the check will fail,
If someone forged my name, the math will tell the tale!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Hash! (The fingerprint!) Sign! (The seal!)
Verify! (Prove that it’s real!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble ends every phrase with the same short signature riff, and after each one the rest of the band checks it by playing it back. Once, Wyrd tries to play the signature on a phrase Nyble didn’t play, and the band refuses to echo it.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Signed! (It came from me!)
Signed! (It’s what I wrote!)
Sign it with my private key and anyone can check the note,
Signed, signed, sealed and true,
Nobody can forge my name, not even you!

songs.note: Every copy of the album was signed with Nyble’s private key. The band signed them with a pen too.
songs.lesson: A cryptographic hash function turns any data into a short, fixed-size fingerprint. It only works one way, and changing even one bit gives a completely different hash. A digital signature is made with the signer’s private key; anyone with the public key can verify who signed the message and that it hasn’t been changed since.

songs.title: Man in the Middle

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: You think you’re talking to me and I think I’m talking to you,
But someone’s in the middle and they’re reading everything we do.
They hand you their key and they tell you it’s mine,
They read it, change it, pass it on, and everything looks fine!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Man in the middle! (Who are you really?)
Man in the middle! (Prove it’s you!)
A public key is only good if you know whose it is,
Man in the middle, and the secret isn’t ours, it’s his!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: So who can vouch the key is mine? A certificate with a name,
Signed by someone that we both trust to guarantee the claim.
Check the certificate, check the chain, before you say hello,
Or you’re whispering your secrets to a stranger you don’t know!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Alice! (To Bob!) Bob! (To Alice!)
Mallory! (Rewriting every scene!)

parts.label: Intercepted solo: Qword, Nyble and Wyrd
parts.desc: Qword and Nyble trade phrases, but every phrase passes through Wyrd’s synth on the way, and Wyrd changes a note or two before passing it on. Neither of them notices until the last exchange, when the phrases no longer match.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Man in the middle! (Who are you really?)
Man in the middle! (Prove it’s you!)
A public key is only good if you know whose it is,
Man in the middle, and the secret isn’t ours, it’s his!

songs.note: The vocals on this one pass through Wyrd’s sampler between Nyble and the microphone. Listen closely, and some words change.
songs.lesson: In a man-in-the-middle attack, an attacker secretly sits between two parties, relaying and possibly changing everything they say, for example by handing each side the attacker’s own public key. The defense is to authenticate keys: certificates signed by trusted certificate authorities bind a public key to a real identity, as SSL (today TLS) does for websites. Alice, Bob and Mallory are cryptography’s classic cast.

songs.title: Social Engineer

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: Every lock we owned was perfect.
Then someone just asked nicely.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: We had the best locks money could buy, the strongest codes around,
Firewalls and passwords, every door was safe and sound.
Then a stranger at the stage door smiled and said, I’m with the duck,
And security just let him in, and that was it for luck!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Social engineer! (Don’t hack the machine!)
Social engineer! (Hack the human in between!)
A friendly voice, a hurried call, a reason to believe,
Social engineer, and it’s people you deceive!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A phone call from the help desk saying they just need your code,
A letter from the boss who needs a payment on the road,
Urgency and authority, the levers that they pull,
Stop and check, call back yourself, and don’t let them fool!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Who’s asking? (Verify!) Why now? (Verify!)
Call them back! (Verify!)
The duck says nothing! (So should I!)

parts.label: The stranger: full band
parts.desc: A stranger’s riff walks into the song mid-solo, confident and friendly, and the whole band starts playing along without checking it. Bytes stops and asks it a question with a single fill. It can’t answer. The band shuts it out and closes the album together.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Social engineer! (Don’t hack the machine!)
Social engineer! (Hack the human in between!)
A friendly voice, a hurried call, a reason to believe,
Social engineer, and it’s people you deceive!

songs.note: About the first night of the 1998 tour, when a fan walked past security by saying “I’m with the duck.” It worked.
songs.lesson: Social engineering attacks people instead of technology: phishing emails, pretexting phone calls, following someone through a locked door, all using urgency and authority to get around good judgment. Defenses include training, verification steps (call back on a number you already know), and systems designed so one person’s mistake can’t compromise everything. People are part of the security system.
